hops.afterHeading: What the bulb sends, and the puzzle
hops.title: The myth of the tiny human olfactory bulb
hops.text: In 1879 French anatomist Paul Broca sorted mammals into those driven mainly by smell and a minority less guided by it. He included semiaquatic carnivores, cetaceans (describing reduced olfactory structures in whales and absent ones in dolphins), and primates including humans, whose large frontal lobes, he argued, let them choose how to respond to odors. His grouping used no smell test, yet the belief that humans smell poorly persisted over a century. In 2008, Yale researchers estimated an average of 5,568 glomeruli per human bulb from sampled sections. Divided by the genomic estimate of about 350 intact receptor types they used, that ratio of totals is roughly 16 to one.

sources.citation: McGann JP (2017) Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth. Science 356(6338):eaam7263.
Maresh A, Rodriguez Gil D, Whitman MC, Greer CA (2008) Principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb: implications for odor processing. PLoS ONE 3(7):e2640.

hops.title: How a fruit fly's smell wiring improved computer search
hops.text: Hashing-based methods that find similar photos or documents, such as conventional locality-sensitive hashing, compress each item into a short code. In 2017 Sanjoy Dasgupta, Charles Stevens and Saket Navlakha pointed out that the fruit fly's smell circuit does the opposite. In their model, signals from about 50 odor channels spread out, largely at random, onto about 2,000 cells, and only the most active 5 percent are kept as the odor's tag. Similar odors end up with overlapping tags. Turned into a search algorithm on three standard benchmarks, this expand-and-sparsify trick beat conventional locality-sensitive hashing. The piriform model in this lesson uses a similar logic: scattered wiring plus a threshold.

sources.citation: Dasgupta S, Stevens CF, Navlakha S (2017) A neural algorithm for a fundamental computing problem. Science 358(6364):793-796.
Salk Institute (2017) Fruit fly brains inform search engines of the future. News release.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small fruit fly sitting on a laptop keyboard beside a ripe banana, facing a screen of clustered photo thumbnails of fruit and flowers.
image.caption: A fly's smell circuit inspired a search algorithm that beat conventional locality-sensitive hashing on three benchmark datasets.

hops.afterHeading: Smell loss in people, and a learned odour map
hops.title: When 'no smell' candle reviews tracked COVID-19 cases
hops.text: During the pandemic, Amazon shoppers kept posting reviews saying their scented candles had no smell. People are often unaware of their own smell loss, so the political scientist Nick Beauchamp asked whether those complaints tracked COVID-19. He collected 9,837 reviews of four best-selling Yankee Candles from late 2018 to late 2021 and adjusted for the rise in 'no smell' reviews that appears every winter. In his model, each extra 100,000 weekly U.S. cases was linked to a rise of about a quarter of a percentage point in the next week's share of no-smell reviews. Perfume reviews showed a weaker hint of the same pattern. Pre-pandemic flu showed none.

sources.citation: Beauchamp N (2022) 'This Candle Has No Smell': detecting the effect of COVID anosmia on Amazon reviews using Bayesian vector autoregression. Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 16(1):1363-1367.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A person seen from behind at a cozy desk, leaning toward a lit glass jar candle beside an open laptop.
image.caption: More reported COVID-19 cases were linked to a larger share of no-smell candle reviews the following week.
